fields.title: Pandita Ramabai (For Teens)
fields.description: At about sixteen, Ramabai watched her father, mother and sister die in a famine, then walked more than four thousand miles with her brother, once sleeping in pits of sand dug on a river bank. A Brahman girl taught Sanskrit when girls were not meant to learn it, she became a famous scholar, a widow at twenty-three, a voice for India's child-widows, and a Christian who said she found the religion eight years before she found Christ. This teen edition tells the true story straight: the losses, the quarrels on every side, the girls rescued from famine and exploitation, and the faith that fed thousands without a bank account.

qa.question: Who was Pandita Ramabai?
qa.answer: An Indian scholar, reformer and Christian, born in 1858 in a forest in the Western Ghats and died in 1922. Orphaned by famine and widowed at twenty-three, she spoke out for the education of women, founded a school for child-widows, rescued thousands of girls from famine at Mukti near Poona, and translated the whole Bible into everyday Marathi.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how her parents and sister died of starvation, how her father meant to drown himself, how her friend took her own life in England, and how girls were exploited in the famine camps, all named plainly but not in detail. It also gives the Hindu reformers who broke with her a fair hearing, and admits where she and her friends got things wrong.

qa.question: What did she mean by “I had not found Christ”?
qa.answer: She wrote that for eight years after her baptism in 1883 she had found the Christian religion, which she believed was true, but had not found Christ, “who is the Life of the religion.” In about 1891 she came to the end of herself and trusted Christ personally as her Saviour, and found that salvation was a free gift, for women as much as for men.

qa.question: Was she the first woman to translate the whole Bible?
qa.answer: Not quite. An American woman, Julia Smith, had published her own English translation of the whole Bible in 1876, and the Marathi Bible had been translated long before by missionaries. Ramabai's was the first whole Bible in plain, everyday Marathi, and she was among the first women anywhere to translate all of Scripture from the original languages.

qa.question: Why did the Hindu reformers who helped her break with her school?
qa.answer: Her school for widows had been promised as neutral in religion, and by 1893 many girls were coming to her morning prayers and reading the Bible. Respected reformers such as Ranade and Bhandarkar felt the promise had been broken and resigned. She answered that nothing was done in secret and no girl was forced, but she would not shut her door. Both sides had a point.

qa.question: How did she treat people who did not share her faith?
qa.answer: She never forced anyone to become a Christian, and she defended the memory of her Hindu parents, who did not know Christ but taught her to love the truth. She was also frank about what she thought was wrong, and in later life she saw little good in the religion she grew up in, which one of her careful biographers thought was a blind spot. At the end, her old Poona friend Ramabai Ranade still came to visit her.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Pandita Ramabai, which draws on her own writings, including The High-Caste Hindu Woman, her account of the famine, A Testimony and her letters, and checks them against the early lives and modern scholars. Stories that admirers added later, and that she never told herself, are left out or marked.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from her story?
qa.answer: That honest questions can lead you to God rather than away from him; that suffering does not automatically make you kind, but grace can; that believing Christianity is true is not the same as trusting Christ; and that instead of wishing someone else would help people in need, you can begin yourself.

fields.title: The Well of Ignorance
fields.body_html:
“And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be upon thy heart; and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.” — Deuteronomy 6:6-7 (ASV)

Pandita Ramabai's story begins with a woman reciting poetry. Anant Shastri Dongre was a Brahman scholar from the Mangalore district of south-western India. As a young man studying in Poona, he heard one of the ruler's wives reciting Sanskrit poems in the palace. It astonished him. The law-books taught that women, like the lowest castes, could not study the Vedas, and most learned men held that women should not learn Sanskrit at all. He decided to teach his own wife. She refused, and so did his family.

Years later, after his first wife died, a father on pilgrimage met him bathing in the river Godavari and offered him his nine-year-old daughter in marriage. Ramabai told the story herself, without names, as an example of how carelessly girls were married off: “All things were settled in an hour or so; next day the marriage was concluded, and the little girl placed in the possession of the stranger, who took her nearly nine hundred miles away from her home.” The stranger, about forty-four, was Anant Shastri. The little girl, Lakshmibai, became Ramabai's mother. Ramabai did not hide her judgement of that careless father, though she admitted “the little girl had fallen in good hands.” Her husband would teach her.

When his family objected again, he took his young wife up to a forest on a peak of the Western Ghats. Summoned before his guru and an assembly of scholars, he defended teaching women from the ancient authorities, and won. “He cared little for what people said, and did what he thought was right,” his daughter wrote. He did not question the Hindu religion; he was “a very orthodox Hindu.” What he rejected was the rule that women must be kept ignorant.

Ramabai was born in that forest in April 1858, the youngest of three surviving children. Her father fed every pilgrim who came, and before she was a year old the money was gone. “She placed me in a big box made of cane,” Ramabai said of her mother, “and a man carried it on his head from the mountain top to the valley. Thus my pilgrim life began when I was a little baby.”

For years the family lived as Puranikas, reading the sacred Puranas aloud in temples and by rivers. At about thirteen she was at Dwarka, where, the legend said, Krishna's golden city would rise from the sea for the sinless once in sixty years. At sunset the clouds glowed gold.

Many people did not dare to say that they did not see the city, for that would be confessing that they were sinners. They kept silence about it and so did we. But we were convinced in our inmost hearts that we saw no city but saw the ordinary clouds which we were accustomed to see, almost daily, at the time of sunset.

And her parents gave her one more gift. Brahman girls were usually married by eight or nine, sometimes as babies. Hers refused. “My father and mother did not do with me as others were in the habit of doing with their daughters,” she said, “i.e., throw me into the well of ignorance by giving me in marriage in my infancy.” It cost her father his standing among the Brahmans.

Moses told the parents of Israel to teach their children “when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way.” Ramabai's parents did not know the God of Israel, but they did exactly that. Long after she left their religion, Ramabai would not let anyone say in her presence that her parents were lost.

Honour what your parents got right, even if you come to believe differently. And remember Dwarka: a whole crowd pretending, because the truth felt shameful. That happens in churches too. God would rather have your honest questions than a polite pretence.

One thing to do this week: tell a parent, grandparent or guardian one thing they taught you that you are glad to know. And notice one moment when you are tempted to pretend, just because everyone else does. Be honest instead.

study_questions.question: Why did Anant Shastri take his young wife into the forest?
study_questions.answer: Because his family objected to him teaching her Sanskrit, and he was determined to go on teaching her whatever people said.

study_questions.question: What did Ramabai mean by “the well of ignorance”?
study_questions.answer: Being married as a small child, which would have ended her education. Her parents refused, even though it cost her father his standing among the Brahmans.

study_questions.question: What happened at Dwarka, and why does it matter?
study_questions.answer: The pilgrims waited to see Krishna's golden city, and the family saw only sunset clouds but kept silent like everyone else. Ramabai learned there that she would rather know the truth than pretend.

fields.title: Sugar and Water
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” — Psalm 27:10 (ASV)

Ramabai was about sixteen when a long famine began in southern India.

She did not blame the weather for all of it. Her father had grown old and blind and lost his wealth. The sacred books promised that if people worshipped in the right ways, gave alms and fasted, the gods would give them what they asked. So the family did exactly that. “For three years we did nothing but perform these religious acts. At last all the money which we had was spent, but the gods did not help us. We suffered from famine, which we had brought upon ourselves.” They sold everything, down to their cooking pots, and gave the money to the priests. Learning an ordinary trade had seemed beneath them, something she later called “the pride of caste and superior learning.”

At the hill shrine of Tirupati, with nothing left, they decided it was better to die in the forest than to bear the disgrace of poverty among their own people. For eleven days they lived on water, leaves and a few wild dates. Then her father, old, blind and starving, decided to drown himself in a sacred pool, which in Hindu belief was not suicide but a holy death. He said goodbye to each child. Ramabai came last. He held her tight and stroked her face. “Remember, my child,” he said, “you are my youngest, my most beloved child. I have given you into the hands of our God. You are His, and to Him alone you must belong and serve all your life.”

Then her brother Srinivas stepped in. He could not watch his father die, he said; they would give up their pride and he would find work. Their father agreed. Even so, Ramabai admitted, “we wished very much that a tiger, a great snake, or some other wild animal would put an end to our lives.”

They dragged themselves to a village. At the start of his last illness, her father “asked for a little sugar and water. We gave him water, but could not give sugar.” He died on the third morning. No one would help carry his body, so Srinivas tied it in his cloth and carried it alone for over two miles.

That evening their mother fell ill. In the town of Raichur, desperately hungry, she sent Ramabai to a neighbour to ask for a piece of coarse millet bread. Ramabai could not make herself beg. “I kept the tears back; but they poured out of my nose instead of my eyes, in spite of me, and the expression of my face told its own story.” The woman understood and gave her the bread. “I ran to my mother in great haste, and gave it to her. But she could not eat, she was too weak.” A few days later her mother died. Soon after, her sister died of starvation too. Only Ramabai and her brother were left.

If you have ever felt, like that family in the forest, that you would rather not go on living, you are not alone, and it is not weakness to say so. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

David wrote, “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” Ramabai's parents had not forsaken her; they loved her to the end. But she came to believe God had taken her up in that forest. “My father's prayers for me were, no doubt, heard by the Almighty,” she wrote.

And the worst days of her life became the root of her life's work. Years later she told her daughter, “When you go to Raichur, think of my mother, and remember that it was there that I got my inspiration for famine work.”

One thing to do this week: this week, give some food, some money or an hour of time to people who feed the hungry where you live.

study_questions.question: How did Ramabai say her family's famine was partly their own doing?
study_questions.answer: They spent all their money on religious acts and gifts to the priests, hoping the gods would make them rich, and their pride of caste kept them from learning ordinary work.

study_questions.question: What were her father's last words to her?
study_questions.answer: That he had given her into the hands of their God, and that she belonged to God and must serve him all her life.

study_questions.question: What did Raichur, where her mother died, come to mean for her?
study_questions.answer: She told her daughter that it was there she got her inspiration for famine work, the rescue of starving people that filled much of her later life.

fields.title: Worse Than Demons
fields.body_html:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” — Ezekiel 36:26 (ASV)

Ramabai and Srinivas were alone. For more than three years they walked. “We had walked more than four thousand miles on foot without any sort of comfort,” she wrote, “sometimes eating what kind people gave us and sometimes going without food.” The figure is her own: from the south to Kashmir and across to Calcutta. Srinivas earned “only four rupees a month, and sometimes much less.”

One freezing night by the Jhelum river in the Punjab, with no blankets, they dug “two gravelike pits,” lay in them, and covered their bodies, “except the heads,” with dry sand. Picture it: the children of a learned scholar, lying in two graves of their own digging.

They kept up their prayers and fasts, but their faith was draining away. “We had fulfilled all the conditions laid down in the sacred books and kept all the rules as far as our knowledge went,” she wrote, “but the gods were not pleased with us and did not appear to us.” (Admirers later added stories about these years, like Ramabai working as a cook. She never told them herself, so they are left out here.)

You might expect her to say that hunger taught her to care for the hungry. She said the opposite.

Yet I must say that suffering alone is not able to produce sympathy for other sufferers. My own experience of the unconverted state of mind, and the present knowledge of my fellow country women and girls, whom I have ample opportunity to study, shows that suffering in itself has rather a hardening effect on the human heart. It takes away almost all delicate feelings from the soul, making it as hard as a stone.

In 1878 they reached Calcutta, the capital of British India. A young woman of about twenty who could recite thousands of Sanskrit verses and compose new ones on the spot caused a sensation. The pandits gave her the title Sarasvati, after the goddess of learning, and she became known as Pandita Ramabai: Ramabai the scholar. (Later claims that she was the first woman ever so honoured cannot be checked.)

Asked to lecture to high-caste women on their duties according to the scriptures, she read the Hindu law-books carefully for the first time. They contradicted each other on almost everything, she found, except two things:

that women of high and low caste, as a class, were bad, very bad, worse than demons, as unholy as untruth; and that they could not get Moksha as men.

Moksha is liberation from the endless round of death and rebirth. A woman's only hope, the books taught, was to worship her husband as a god and be born a man in some later life. “I wanted something more than the Shastras could give me,” she wrote, “but I did not know what it was that I wanted.”

In Calcutta she also met Christians for the first time. They gave her a Bible in Sanskrit. She thought reading it was “quite a waste of time,” and yet, “I have never parted with it since then.” And when she told the famous reformer Keshab Chandra Sen that women were not allowed to read the Vedas, he only smiled and gave her one. It was permission to think for herself.

What Ramabai said about suffering is worth remembering. People sometimes say hard times make you a better person. Sometimes they just make you colder and more guarded. She believed what changed her heart was not suffering but grace: God doing what Ezekiel promised, taking away “the stony heart” and giving “a heart of flesh.”

One thing to do this week: think of one way something hard has made you colder toward other people. Ask God honestly to soften that place, then do one small kindness this week for someone you would usually ignore.

study_questions.answer: It was freezing and they had no blankets, so they lay in pits and covered themselves with sand to keep warm.

study_questions.answer: It hardens it, “making it as hard as a stone.” She believed only God's grace could make her heart tender again.

study_questions.question: What did she find in the Hindu law-books about women?
study_questions.answer: That they all agreed women were “worse than demons” and could not attain moksha, liberation, as men could; their only hope was to serve their husbands and be born men in a later life.

fields.title: Nineteen Months
fields.body_html:
“For thy Maker is thy husband; Jehovah of hosts is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is thy Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called.” — Isaiah 54:5 (ASV)

In 1880 Srinivas fell ill and died. His only worry was what would happen to his sister, alone in the world.

When he spoke of his anxiety, I answered: “There is no one but God to care for you and me.” “Ah,” he answered, “then if God cares for us, I am afraid of nothing.”

She was twenty-two. Her father, mother, sister and brother were gone.

Six months later she married Bipin Behari Medhavi, a Bengali lawyer and a friend of her brother's. He was not a Brahman, and to orthodox Brahmans such a marriage was a scandal. She said plainly why she did it: “Having lost all faith in the religion of my ancestors I married a Bengali gentleman of the Shudra caste.” They had a civil ceremony, because “We neither of us believed either in Hinduism or Christianity.” They made a home in Silchar, in Assam, and in 1881 their longed-for daughter was born. They named her Manorama, “heart's joy.”

At Silchar, Ramabai found a little pamphlet in her library. She never knew how it got there. It was Luke's Gospel in Bengali. A Baptist missionary, Mr. Allen, explained the first chapter of Genesis to her. “It struck me as being a true story,” she said, “but I could not give any reason for thinking so or believing in it.” When she told her husband she would become a Christian if she became sure it was true, he was angry. He had defied his caste to marry her, but joining “the despised Christian community” was too far. “I do not know just what would have happened had he lived,” she wrote.

He did not live. Early in 1882 he died of cholera. She remembered “nineteen months of happy married life,” though scholars' dates suggest it was a little shorter. “I was left alone to face the world with one baby in my arms.”

Here is what being a widow meant in high-caste Hindu society then. A widow was blamed for her husband's death, through sins in this life or a former one. She could not remarry. Her head was shaved, her jewellery taken, and she ate one meal a day. She was kept away from weddings as unlucky. Child-widows, girls married as small children whose husbands died, lived this way from childhood to old age. Ramabai, who had married outside Hindu custom, was spared most of it. But she knew it from the inside. She was twenty-three, with no family and no home.

What she said next is remarkable for someone who was not yet a Christian. “This great grief drew me nearer to God. I felt that He was teaching me, and that if I was to come to Him, He must Himself draw me.”

She did not know who God was yet. But she had grasped something many people take years to learn: you cannot find your own way to God; he comes looking for you. Jesus said the same: “No man can come to me, except the Father that sent me draw him.”

In the world she grew up in, a woman's husband was her god, and when he died her hope died with him. Isaiah says something completely different to a people pictured as a widow: “For thy Maker is thy husband.” A widow is not cursed, and she is not alone. Ramabai would spend her life telling that to the widows of India. First she had to learn it herself.

Loss can make people run from God or toward him. If you are grieving right now, you don't have to have it figured out. You can tell God what she came to see: if I am to come to you, you will have to draw me.

fields.title: Open Thy Mouth for the Dumb
fields.body_html:
“Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate.” — Proverbs 31:8 (ASV)

In 1882, with her baby, Ramabai moved to Poona, where her father had first heard a woman reciting Sanskrit. The city was divided. Reformers like the judge Mahadev Govind Ranade and the scholar R. G. Bhandarkar worked carefully for women's education and the remarriage of widows; the orthodox saw every change as an attack on Hindu society. The reformers welcomed her. Ranade's young wife said she had “amazing skill in winning the hearts of her hearers.”

Within months Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj, a society of women working to free women from child-marriage and “the bondage of ignorance.” It was one of the first organisations in India founded and led by a woman for women, and she did not soften her words. “Men look on us women as chattels,” she said. “We make every effort to deliver ourselves from this situation. But some will say that this is a rebellion against man, and that to do this is sin. To leave men's evil acts unrebuked and remain unmoved before them is a great sin.” The orthodox newspapers attacked her almost at once.

That September a British commission came to Poona to look into education in India. Ramabai, twenty-four, with no degree and no position, gave evidence. “I consider it my duty,” she said, “to the very end of my life, to maintain this cause, and to advocate the proper position of women in this land.”

In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, the educated men of this country are opposed to Female Education and the proper position of woman. ... It is evident that women, being one-half of the people of this country, are oppressed and cruelly treated by the other half.

She asked for women doctors, because most Indian women “would rather die than speak of their ailments to a man.” The chairman had her evidence translated and printed.

That year a child-widow of about twelve was brought to her. She had been married at five, and her boy husband had died a few days after the wedding. Her mother-in-law would not look at her. “She said the girl had eaten up her son and was a great demon.” Ramabai took the girl in. “As I looked on that little figure,” she wrote, “my vague thoughts about doing something for my sisters in similar conditions began to take shape.” She would open a home for widows. When no one would fund it, she decided to train as a doctor in England.

For a high-caste Hindu, crossing the sea meant losing caste. For a widow to go with a toddler was almost unheard of. In the spring of 1883 she sailed anyway, with two-year-old Manorama and a young friend, Anandibai Bhagat. She was still not a Christian, though she had been reading the New Testament with an English missionary and listening to Father Nehemiah Goreh, a gentle Indian priest who, like her, had been born a Brahman.

Proverbs says, “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate.” In that old English, “dumb” means people who cannot speak. The child-widow could not speak for herself. Ramabai could, so she did.

You probably have more voice than someone near you: a kid who gets mocked, a classmate who can't speak the language well, someone being piled on online. Speaking up rarely makes you popular. Ramabai was attacked in the papers within weeks. But she knew that staying silent about wrong was its own kind of sin.

One thing to do this week: find one situation this week where someone is being treated unfairly and can't easily defend themselves. Say one true, calm sentence on their behalf, to the person doing it, to an adult who can help, or to the person being hurt.

fields.title: The Woman at the Well
fields.body_html:
“but whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall become in him a well of water springing up unto eternal life.” — John 4:14 (ASV)

“The voice came to me as to Abraham,” Ramabai said later. “I went forth as Abraham, not knowing whither I went.” In England, Anglican sisters at Wantage, near Oxford, took her in, and one of them, almost certainly Sister Geraldine, became her “spiritual mother” and taught her English.

Then came two hard blows. Ramabai was already partly deaf, and she was told her deafness made it impossible to train as a doctor. She had crossed the sea for nothing, it seemed. Worse, a few months after they arrived, her friend Anandibai Bhagat took her own life. The reasons have never been clear. Some at the time suggested she feared being pressed to become a Christian; others saw other causes. Ramabai's published accounts never mention it. At twenty-five she had lost her parents, her sister, her brother, her husband and the friend who came with her. For a time, it seems, she was badly shaken.

If you have lost someone to suicide, or are struggling with thoughts of ending your life, please don't carry it alone. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

Then, in London, the sisters took her to a rescue home at Fulham, run by Christians for women who had been prostitutes. Many of those women now nursed the sick.

Here for the first time in my life, I came to know that something should be done to reclaim the so-called fallen women, and that Christians, whom Hindus considered outcasts and cruel, were kind to these unfortunate women, degraded in the eyes of society.

She had never seen anyone treat such women kindly. She asked what made Christians care for them. The sister read her John 4, the story of Jesus and the Samaritan woman at the well. The woman belonged to a despised people. She had had five husbands. She came to the well alone at midday. And Jesus spoke to her, told her the truth about her life without condemning her, and offered her “living water.”

She spoke of the Infinite Love of Christ for sinners. He did not despise them but came to save them. I had never read or heard anything like this in the religious books of the Hindus. I realized, after reading the fourth chapter of St. John's Gospel, that Christ was truly the Divine Saviour He claimed to be, and no one but He could transform and uplift the downtrodden womanhood of India, and of every land.

“Thus my heart was drawn to the religion of Christ.” Her mind still needed reasons. They came from a book by Father Goreh on Hindu philosophy. “I was intellectually convinced of its truth on reading a book written by Father Goreh.” She needed both: an English sister showing her Christians who cared for outcasts, and an Indian Brahman convert showing her, in her own tradition of thought, why Christianity was true.

On 29 September 1883 she was baptised at Wantage, with Manorama, and took the name Mary. She was calm, not ecstatic. “I knew full well that it would displease my friends and my countrymen very much; but I have never regretted having taken the step.” Back in Poona, many were dismayed. For some of her countrymen, she has never been forgiven.

People come to faith by different roads. Some are moved by love they see in action; some need to think it through. Ramabai needed both, and God gave her both. If you're still asking questions, that's not a problem. And if you are a Christian, remember: someone may be watching how you treat the people everyone else looks down on, to decide whether Jesus is real.

One thing to do this week: read John 4:1-42 this week, the whole story. Notice how Jesus treats the woman, and write down one thing he does that surprises you.

study_questions.answer: Jesus spoke kindly to a despised woman with a bad reputation and offered her living water, when the books Ramabai knew said women were worse than demons.

study_questions.answer: Her heart was drawn by Christians' love for outcast women and by John 4, and her mind was convinced by Father Goreh's book.

fields.title: Out of Nazareth
fields.body_html:
“prove all things; hold fast that which is good;” — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (ASV)

Baptism did not stop Ramabai asking questions. At Cheltenham Ladies' College, where she had the first formal schooling of her life, she sat in Bible class “with her aurophone touching her teeth,” following every word. She also argued. She questioned the Trinity and eternal punishment, kept her vegetarian diet, and asked why she should accept one church's teaching when Christians disagreed so much. The sisters, who loved her, saw much of this as pride. She answered that “the door of the Universal Church of God is not shut against me.” She was proud in a way, and she was also right not to be run by people who did not understand her country. Her answer to the confusion was simple: “I determined not to take the opinion of men as my ground of belief, and went on reading the Bible only.”

In 1886 she sailed to America for the graduation of a relative, Anandibai Joshee, the first Indian woman to graduate in medicine from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania. She meant to stay a few weeks. She stayed nearly three years. There she wrote The High-Caste Hindu Woman, a short, angry book about a woman's life from birth to death: child marriage, life as a servant in her husband's family, and above all the life of the widow. She did not spare the British: “under the so-called Christian British rule, the woman is in no better condition than of old.” It ended with a plan: a school where high-caste widows could train as teachers and earn their living with dignity.

Before one journey, a friend asked for a message for her readers.

“Remind them,” she replied, with animated countenance and rapid speech, as she clasped my hand, “that it was 'out of Nazareth' that the blessed Redeemer of mankind came; that great reforms have again and again been wrought by instrumentalities that the world despised. Tell them to help me educate the high-caste child-widows; for I solemnly believe that this hated and despised class of women, educated and enlightened, are, by God's grace, to redeem India!”

Supporters in Boston formed the Ramabai Association to back the school for ten years. Then, afraid of the welcome waiting at home, she knelt, “committed myself to the care of our loving heavenly Father and sailed.”

On 11 March 1889 she opened Sharada Sadan, the Home of Wisdom, in Bombay. It was not a Christian school. She had promised it would be neutral in religion, and the girls kept their caste rules. But each morning she read the Bible and prayed with Manorama in her own room, and she left the door open. Girls began to peep in, then to sit, then to stay.

“These are my own private prayers,” explained Pandita Ramabai. “No girl is compelled to come in; but one by one they have come of their own accord.”

That December, at the Indian National Congress, men crowded forward to hear her. She began: “It is not strange, my countrymen, that my voice is small, for you have never given a woman the chance to make her voice strong!”

The open door was honest. It was also the beginning of a storm, because Hindu parents had been promised a neutral school.

Paul told the Thessalonians to “prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” Ramabai did. She didn't swallow everything her teachers said, and she didn't throw out her faith because Christians disagreed. She went to the Bible itself. If you are full of questions, that is a good model. Doubt that sends you to the source can lead somewhere.

One thing to do this week: pick one thing you believe about God mainly because someone told you. Find where the Bible talks about it, read the passage for yourself, and write down what it actually says.

study_questions.answer: That Jesus came from a despised town, and God often works through people the world despises. She believed the hated child-widows, once educated, could help renew India.

study_questions.question: What was the “open door” at Sharada Sadan?
study_questions.answer: She prayed and read the Bible in her own room each morning with the door open, and girls were free to come in if they wished. No one was made to come.

fields.title: Building from the Top
fields.body_html:
“The people that sat in darkness Saw a great light, And to them that sat in the region and shadow of death, To them did light spring up.” — Matthew 4:16 (ASV)

While all this went on in public, a quieter story was happening in private. Ramabai later said it was the most important thing that happened to her in those years.

She had been a Christian for about six years. She had been baptised, argued theology, lectured on Christian love and founded a school. But for years, she said, she had studied “other books about the Bible,” not the Bible itself. Back in India she put the other books aside and read Scripture. It made her miserable. “Following this course for about two years I became very unhappy in my mind. I was dissatisfied with my spiritual condition.”

Then, at a mission press in Bombay, she picked up a book by an English clergyman, William Haslam. He had had a good parish and been busy with every kind of church activity, until a woman told him he was “trying to build from the top.” She meant he had never been converted. He had the religion without the life.

That hit Ramabai hard. “There were so many things I did not understand intellectually. One thing I knew by this time, that I needed Christ, and not merely His religion.” Looking honestly at herself, she saw that “sin had dominion over me.” She became restless, almost ill, and spent many sleepless nights. Then:

I had at last come to an end of myself, and unconditionally surrendered myself to the Saviour, and asked Him to be merciful to me and to become my Righteousness and Redemption, and to take away all my sin.

She dated it to 1891, eight years after her baptism, and would not describe the moment. What mattered was the result. “I came to know, after eight years from the time of my baptism, that I had found the Christian religion, which was good enough for me; but I had not found Christ, who is the Life of the religion.” She compared herself to the blind man in John 9 whose eyes were opened: she had been “sitting in darkness,” and “saw great light.”

What amazed her most was that salvation was free, and that it was for women. All her life she had been taught that everything had to be earned, by pilgrimages, fasting, gifts to priests, serving a husband as a god, and that liberation was not open to women at all. Even her early Christian faith, she realised, had been mixed with the idea that she must earn forgiveness. Now she read: “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

How good, how indescribably good! What good news — for me, a woman; a woman born in India among Brahmins, who hold out no hope for me and the like of me.

“No caste, no sex, no work, and no man was to be depended upon to get salvation, this everlasting life; but God gave it freely to any one and every one who believed on His Son.”

Everything she did afterwards flowed from this. The famine children, the widows, the women rescued from the streets would not have to earn anything. Neither had she.

You can grow up in church, know the songs, believe the right things, even serve, and still be “building from the top.” Ramabai was not a fake; she really believed. But believing Christianity is true is not the same as trusting Christ himself. And this is not a test you fail by being honest. Her turning point came when she stopped pretending she was fine.

One thing to do this week: ask yourself Ramabai's question: have I found Christ, or only the Christian religion? Write your honest answer down. If you're not sure, tell God that in plain words, and talk to someone you trust about it.

study_questions.question: What did “trying to build from the top” mean?
study_questions.answer: Having the religion without the life: being busy with church and believing the creed without ever personally turning to Christ.

study_questions.question: What difference did Ramabai see between “the Christian religion” and “Christ”?
study_questions.answer: For eight years she believed Christianity was true and practised it, but had not personally trusted Christ as her Saviour, “the Life of the religion.”

study_questions.question: Why was the free gift of salvation such good news for her as a woman?
study_questions.answer: She had been taught that liberation was closed to women and that everything had to be earned. In Christ she found salvation given freely to anyone, whatever their caste or sex.

fields.body_text: “The people that sat in darkness Saw a great light, And to them that sat in the region and shadow of death, To them did light spring up.” — Matthew 4:16 (ASV) While all this went on in public, a quieter story was happening in private. Ramabai later said it was the most important thing that happened to her in those years. She had been a Christian for about six years. She had been baptised, argued theology, lectured on Christian love and founded a school. But for years, she said, she had studied “other books about the Bible,” not the Bible itself. Back in India she put the other books aside and read Scripture. It made her miserable. “Following this course for about two years I became very unhappy in my mind. I was dissatisfied with my spiritual condition.” Then, at a mission press in Bombay, she picked up a book by an English clergyman, William Haslam. He had had a good parish and been busy with every kind of church activity, until a woman told him he was “trying to build from the top.” She meant he had never been converted. He had the religion without the life. That hit Ramabai hard. “There were so many things I did not understand intellectually. One thing I knew by this time, that I needed Christ, and not merely His religion.” Looking honestly at herself, she saw that “sin had dominion over me.” She became restless, almost ill, and spent many sleepless nights. Then: I had at last come to an end of myself, and unconditionally surrendered myself to the Saviour, and asked Him to be merciful to me and to become my Righteousness and Redemption, and to take away all my sin. She dated it to 1891, eight years after her baptism, and would not describe the moment. What mattered was the result. “I came to know, after eight years from the time of my baptism, that I had found the Christian religion, which was good enough for me; but I had not found Christ, who is the Life of the religion.” She compared herself to the blind man in John 9 whose eyes were opened: she had been “sitting in darkness,” and “saw great light.” What amazed her most was that salvation was free, and that it was for women. All her life she had been taught that everything had to be earned, by pilgrimages, fasting, gifts to priests, serving a husband as a god, and that liberation was not open to women at all. Even her early Christian faith, she realised, had been mixed with the idea that she must earn forgiveness. Now she read: “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” How good, how indescribably good! What good news — for me, a woman; a woman born in India among Brahmins, who hold out no hope for me and the like of me. “No caste, no sex, no work, and no man was to be depended upon to get salvation, this everlasting life; but God gave it freely to any one and every one who believed on His Son.” Everything she did afterwards flowed from this. The famine children, the widows, the women rescued from the streets would not have to earn anything. Neither had she. You can grow up in church, know the songs, believe the right things, even serve, and still be “building from the top.” Ramabai was not a fake; she really believed. But believing Christianity is true is not the same as trusting Christ himself. And this is not a test you fail by being honest. Her turning point came when she stopped pretending she was fine. One thing to do this week: ask yourself Ramabai's question: have I found Christ, or only the Christian religion? Write your honest answer down. If you're not sure, tell God that in plain words, and talk to someone you trust about it.

fields.title: The Storm of 1893
fields.body_html:
“What time I am afraid, I will put my trust in thee.” — Psalm 56:3 (ASV)

By 1893 the school had moved to Poona and had more than sixty pupils, most of them widows, and more and more were coming to Ramabai's morning prayers. According to Helen Dyer, one holiday about thirty chose a day of prayer over a picnic, and more than twenty said they wanted to learn about Christ. Nothing was done in secret. That was exactly the problem.

On 13 August 1893 three Hindu gentlemen who had lent their names to the school resigned. Two of them, Ranade and Bhandarkar, had welcomed her to Poona eleven years before. Their letter put their case fairly. The school had “departed from the lines of strict neutrality on which the institution was started,” they wrote. “If the Sadana is to be conducted as an avowed proselytizing institution, we must disavow all connection with it.”

Anonymous letters threatened her life. Parents took thirty-one girls home. She kept track of every one.

It would be easy to tell this as a simple story of a faithful Christian and her persecutors. It wasn't. Ranade and Bhandarkar were among the most open-minded Hindus of their day. They had risked their own standing for women's education, and backed Ramabai when few others would, on the understanding that the school would not make converts. They believed, with reason, that the understanding had been broken.

Ramabai told her side plainly. “We did nothing in secret. My room was always open. They asked me whether some of the girls attended my private prayers. I replied that they did. They then asked me to prevent them from doing so. I told them I could not conscientiously do that.” The Bible was never a school subject, and no girl was made to come.

Both sides had a point. A school run by a devout, persuasive Christian with an open door could not be neutral in the way Hindu parents understood. But Ramabai had forced no one, and she would not shut her door against a girl who wanted to pray. The promise had been made in good faith, in America, by people who did not see what it would mean in Poona.

Some of her friends behaved worse than she did. When one girl's mother came to reclaim her, though the girl did not want to go back, some of Ramabai's supporters hid her, kept Ramabai herself in the dark, and had her baptised without Ramabai's consent. Ramabai begged for the girl to be produced. It is to her credit that she wanted the girl returned, and to her friends' discredit that they did not listen. It also shows why Hindu parents feared her school.

What kept her going? According to Dyer, one promise that came to her that year was from Isaiah: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper.” She was a woman alone, attacked by the leading men of her own people, her school half empty. She did not pretend not to be afraid. She trusted anyway. Later she said she had been delivered twice: “first delivered from the slavery of man's opinions, from the fear of man which holds so many of my dear people, and a second time from the bondage of sin.”

Two years later some girls asked to be baptised. Six wrote to Boston: “This we have done out of our own free choice. No human being could have wrought this change in us, and no one could have induced us to become Christians.”

Being open about your faith can cost you friends, even good ones who are partly right. The answer is not to hide your faith, or to pretend the other side has no point. It is to be open, fair and unafraid. “What time I am afraid, I will put my trust in thee.”

One thing to do this week: think of someone who disagrees with you about faith or something important. Write down the strongest fair point they could make. Then, if the chance comes, listen to them properly before you answer.

study_questions.answer: That nothing was done in secret, her room was always open and no girl was forced, but she could not in conscience stop girls who wanted to come to her prayers.

study_questions.question: What did she say she had been “delivered” from twice?
study_questions.answer: First from “the slavery of man's opinions,” the fear of what people think, and second from “the bondage of sin.”

fields.title: Remember the Days of Old
fields.body_html:
“Remember the days of old, Consider the years of many generations: Ask thy father, and he will show thee; Thine elders, and they will tell thee.” — Deuteronomy 32:7 (ASV)

In 1896 the rains failed and famine spread across the Central Provinces. Ramabai did not want to go. She was thirty-eight, partly deaf and tired, and her school was still recovering. She argued with herself: “what can a weak woman do to help the dying thousands?” Others were helping. “There is nothing for you to do.”

“I tried to quiet my conscience in this manner,” she wrote, “but louder and louder spoke the voice of God from within my heart: 'Remember the days of old'.” She remembered her father in the forest and her mother at Raichur. She had been a famine child herself. “I could no longer keep still.”

At Sohagpur she saw three small children outside the hospital, crying for food. Their mother had died the day before. Thinking she needed official permission to take them, she went to find the officer. When she came back they were gone. She never found them. “The memory of the three little ones, especially of the youngest child, who, I am sure, could not have lived many days after that, haunts me to this day.” She did not blame the officials. She blamed herself.

In the relief camps, she said, some officials were kind, but many overseers stole the food and abused the people. Worst of all, girls and young widows were being lured away and sold into prostitution. In one camp a girl of about fourteen told her she was “kept” there by someone. An old woman explained what that meant. The official in charge of the district, when told, “nodded his head, and said that it is quite possible that such things are happening in the poorhouses, but he cannot help it.”

Ramabai would not accept that. She even warned the British rulers, who had once licensed prostitution for their soldiers and were under pressure to do it again, that if they did, “British iniquity will reach its climax.” Her admiring British biographers left that line out. Being a Christian, to her, did not mean excusing a Christian nation's sins against Indian women.

“The Lord has put it into my mind to save three hundred girls out of the famine districts,” she wrote, “and I shall go to work in His name.” She did not have the money. “I do not know, but the Lord knows what I need.”

On one journey home, a hungry girl picked some green gram, a kind of bean, from a field. Ramabai made her give it back. When the ringleader later ran away and was brought back, Ramabai decided to make an example of her and leave her behind. The carts started. The girl sat down on the ground in the dusk.

The world seemed very, very wide; and on it was thrown one little girl, friendless, homeless, and helpless. The picture is everlastingly engraved on my heart. ... The sad picture was too much, too much for me. I ordered the driver to stop the cart, for I could not move an inch from that place.

Sitting there, she thought of how often she had gone her own way, and how often God had called her back: “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” She waved. The girl saw the hand “and at once bounded and ran toward me.” Her name was Girija, “a child of the mountain.”

It is a story about a hard woman learning to be soft, and she told it against herself. By the rules, she was right to leave the girl. She was also wrong. God had not waited for her to prove she was sorry before he called her.

She would not tell herself it was someone else's problem; what she had suffered became the reason she acted. And she was honest about her failures. You can be someone who acts and someone who admits where you got it wrong.

One thing to do this week: think of a time someone gave you a second chance you didn't deserve. This week, give someone else one: a friend, a sibling, someone who annoyed you. Call them back instead of driving off.

study_questions.question: Why did Ramabai feel she had to go into the famine districts?
study_questions.answer: God reminded her to “remember the days of old.” She had been a famine child herself and could not sit comfortably while other children starved.

study_questions.question: What did the girl mean when she said she was “kept” in the poorhouse?
study_questions.answer: That a man was holding her there and sexually exploiting her. The official who was told said he could not help it.

study_questions.question: What did Ramabai learn from Girija?
study_questions.answer: That as God had loved her and called her back while she was still a sinner, she should call back the wandering girl instead of waiting for proof that she was sorry.

fields.title: The Sweeper
fields.body_html:
“Bring ye the whole tithe into the store-house, that there may be food in my house, and prove me now herewith, saith Jehovah of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.” — Malachi 3:10 (ASV)

When Ramabai brought her famine girls back to Poona in 1897, bubonic plague had reached the city. The magistrate ordered her to remove more than a hundred girls within forty-eight hours. “To have brought the girls here to save them from starvation and death,” she wrote bitterly, “was my great sin.” They camped in the open in fierce heat, and some died. The only place left was a bare farm the school owned at Kedgaon, some thirty-five or forty miles away. The girls lived in sheds fenced with thorn bushes. That was the beginning of Mukti.

She had read about George Müller, who cared for thousands of orphans in England without asking anyone but God for money. She wished someone would start such a work in India. Then, she said, she was rebuked:

Then the Lord said to me, “Why don't you begin to do this yourself, instead of wishing for others to do it? How easy it is for any one to wish that some one else would do a difficult thing instead of doing it himself.”

So she did. She named the settlement Mukti. In Hindu thought, mukti means liberation from the endless cycle of births and deaths, the very thing she had been taught a woman could never reach. To her it now meant salvation in Christ, freely given.

Mukti had no endowment, no guaranteed income and no bank account. More and more, Ramabai stopped asking people for money at all. She prayed, told what God had done, and waited. “I own nothing on earth except a few clothes and my Bible,” she wrote. It was not always easy. Once, in a crisis, she stopped her workers' salaries and asked them to trust God as she did, and some of the best left. Living by faith can become a burden on other people too. But for twenty-five years, through famine, plague and war, the people at Mukti were fed. “I have responded to the Lord's challenge, 'Prove Me now',” she wrote, “and have found Him faithful and true.”

In 1899 she laid the foundation stone of Kripa Sadan, the House of Grace, a home where women and girls who had been sexually exploited could be cared for without shame. There was “not a single pice in hand” to build it. It was built anyway, and sheltered hundreds of women most of society treated as beyond help.

Famine struck Gujarat that year, and by August 1900 more than thirteen hundred and fifty Gujarati girls had come to Mukti. Many were ill, and many died. But a visitor in 1901 found some two thousand women and girls living in stone buildings, with schools, a hospital, workrooms and a church. “Five years ago,” he wrote, “there was nothing here but an open field.” The girls learned to read, farm, weave and print.

When a new missionary arrived in 1901, Ramabai told her:

I am a sweeper; that is all I am. I sweep into this compound as many as I can get; child-widows, deserted wives, and orphans of every kind, and I want you missionaries to preach to them.

In India, sweeping was work for the lowest castes. For a Brahman woman honoured by the scholars of Calcutta to call herself a sweeper turned everything she had been raised to believe upside down. It was also exactly what she did.

Not everyone saw it that way. To many Hindus, Mukti was a place where famine children, who could not really choose, were made into Christians. That is a fair question, still asked today. Ramabai never hid that she hoped they would believe. What she would not accept was that the gospel made them outcasts. In her eyes they had been outcasts already. Now they had a home.

One thing to do this week: instead of wishing someone would meet a need you've noticed, take one small first step yourself this week, even if it is one phone call or one hour of help.

study_questions.answer: That she gathered in the people society had thrown away, taking the lowest place even though she was a Brahman and an honoured scholar.

fields.title: Fire
fields.body_html:
“Yea and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days Will I pour forth of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy.” — Acts 2:18 (ASV)

The Boston Association had promised to support a neutral school for ten years. By 1898 its own committee wrote that the school had become “a Christian institution,” and Ramabai had taken in hundreds of famine girls without asking. Had she been straightforward? Honestly, she had changed, and so had her work, and she had not asked permission first. She went to Boston and told them plainly. Forty-eight girls had chosen baptism. She gave an account of the money and offered back the buildings and farm it had paid for. Then she told them not to build on her: “Ramabai is dead. ... Do not concentrate your interest in one person, for that person will die and be gone.” A new association was formed, and it supported her for the rest of her life.

On her way home she spoke at the Keswick Convention in England. “Five minutes were given me to speak, and I made the very best use of them.” She asked them to pray “that 100,000 men and 100,000 women from among the Indian Christians may be led to preach the Gospel to their country people.” Women as well as men.

Seven years later, the answer began. In January 1905, after news of a revival in Wales, she asked who would meet every morning to pray. About seventy came forward. They prayed “for the true conversion of all the Indian Christians, including ourselves.” Including ourselves. They did not treat revival as something other people needed. By June, Dyer records, five hundred and fifty were meeting twice a day.

Late in June, an older girl woke the American missionary Minnie Abrams: another girl had received the Holy Spirit. “I saw the fire, ran across the room for a pail of water, and was about to pour it over her when I discovered she was not on fire.” The next evening, while Ramabai was teaching quietly, the whole congregation broke into prayer so loudly that she had to stop. Girls wept and confessed their sins. Stolen things were returned. Girls who had come out of famine and abuse were filled with joy. A worker wrote of a twelve-year-old whose plain face had become radiant without her knowing it: “She is occupied with Jesus.”

Ramabai prayed with them, but quietly. She did not lead the dramatic side of the revival, and she did not stop it. She took a band of girls to Poona and confessed in public that she had “neglected her opportunities of preaching Christ boldly.” Then praying bands went out across western India, and in time more than twenty-nine thousand people were being prayed for by name at Mukti. “When we were Hindus,” she explained, “we used to repeat one or two thousand names of the gods daily. ... Why should we not, as Christians, be able to pray for many hundreds of people by name?”

The Mukti revival began nearly a year before the famous Azusa Street meetings in Los Angeles, often counted as the start of Pentecostalism. Speaking in tongues came to Mukti only later, after news of Azusa Street arrived. Ramabai never made it a test of anything:

Love, perfect divine love, is the only and most necessary sign of the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

Peter, quoting Joel, said God would pour out his Spirit “on my servants and on my handmaidens.” In the world Ramabai grew up in, a woman was forbidden even to study the Vedas. At Mukti the Spirit fell first on famine orphans and former child-widows, and they went out to pray and preach.

Real revival, the Mukti kind, starts with “including ourselves.” It looks like confession, giving back what you took and praying for people by name. Its sign is not noise but love.

fields.title: Having Nothing
fields.body_html:
“as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” — 2 Corinthians 6:10 (ASV)

Ramabai owed her faith, as she saw it, to a book. So she gave her last years to translating the whole Bible into Marathi. Missionaries had translated it long before, but in high, literary language full of Sanskrit words that village women could not follow. She wanted “the simplest form of Marathi speech.” She learned Greek and Hebrew, with help from her students and from members of the Bene Israel, an ancient Jewish community of western India. How much of the final text was her own work and how much she supervised is not entirely clear. She thought it would take seven years. It took more than fourteen. The girls at Mukti printed it themselves, and she never allowed it to be sold. She had received the Bible as a gift, so she gave it freely.

One careful biographer thought something was lost in these years. Once she had defended her parents' faith; later she saw almost nothing good in it, and for years would not let Sanskrit be taught at Mukti. Great Christians can have blind spots. It is also fair to remember what she had seen done to women in the name of religion.

Her daughter Manorama grew up sharing her mother with hundreds of other girls. Whatever she felt, she did not record it. She gave her life to her mother's work. At nineteen she took charge of the school, and later she led praying bands and started a school of her own. Everyone expected her to carry Mukti on.

In July 1921 Manorama was taken to hospital and an operation was attempted, but, as Clementina Butler, who knew them both, wrote, “her heart was not equal to the strain.” She was forty. Ramabai was sixty-three, nearly deaf, and dependent on her daughter for almost everything. Her letter was short: “All I have to say is 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away, Blessed be the name of the Lord.'”

She lived less than nine months longer. She set her house in order and named an English friend, Lissa Hastie, to carry the work on “on exactly the same lines.” Days before she died, too weak to speak, she wrote to the Bible Society's secretary: “I have been a Christian for thirty-eight years. I have found a great salvation through the Society's work. God bless you and yours.”

She died in her sleep at Mukti on 5 April 1922, shortly after the translation was finished. The cable to America said: “Ramabai Promoted.” Young women carried her plain coffin, and a thousand girls followed. All day people came from villages she had fed in every famine since 1896. High castes, low castes and outcastes stood together by the body of a Brahman woman who, in her youth, would have been polluted by the touch of most of them. An old Brahman widow leaned over her and cried, “O, Great Mother, Great Mother, whom now shall I call Mother? Who will care for me?” The poet Sarojini Naidu, who was not a Christian, called her “the first Christian to be enrolled in the calendar of Hindu saints.”

Mukti still stands at Kedgaon, still caring for girls and women.

Paul described the Christian life as “having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” Ramabai lost her family's wealth in a famine and her honour among her own people. She owned a few clothes and a Bible. She left behind a Bible in the language of village women, and thousands of women and girls who had been given back their lives.

She would not want to be remembered as a heroine. She called herself a sweeper, and she would want you to remember God. “I have come to believe the Word of God implicitly,” she wrote, “and I have found out by experience that it is true.” Then she turned to her readers: “I entreat you, my readers, to prove the Lord as I have proved Him.”

One thing to do this week: choose one promise of God in the Bible and “prove” it this week: act on it in one specific way, and keep a note of what happens.

study_questions.answer: With Job's words, “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away, Blessed be the name of the Lord,” and she kept working until her own death less than nine months later.
